article.headline: America's Last Electrical-Steel Maker and the Transformer Bottleneck
article.lede: The United States power grid has a supply problem measured in years: demand for transformers now runs 30% ahead of domestic production capacity, with lead times for large units approaching four years. At the center of the bottleneck is a single material — grain-oriented electrical steel — produced in North America by exactly one company, Cleveland-Cliffs.
article.body:
Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF) is the **sole North American producer of *grain-oriented electrical steel*** (GOES), a silicon-iron alloy whose crystalline grains are aligned during rolling to channel magnetic flux with minimal energy loss — the property that makes transformer cores efficient. Cleveland-Cliffs arrived at this position not by building but by buying: when it acquired AK Steel in March 2020 for roughly $3 billion, the Butler, Pennsylvania and Zanesville, Ohio mills were already the last remaining GOES producers on the continent, as a subsequent U.S. Department of Commerce investigation confirmed. The two facilities together produce up to 250,000 net tons of GOES per year.

That monopoly sits atop a market in acute distress. Power transformer lead times in the United States now average 128 weeks — nearly two and a half years — with large *generator step-up* (GSU) units stretching to 144 weeks and high-capacity units reaching four years. Wood Mackenzie has quantified a **30% supply deficit** in the power-transformer market and a 10% shortfall in distribution transformers; prices have risen 77–95% since 2019 depending on type. More than 55% of distribution transformers already in service exceed their expected design life, making replacement demand structural rather than cyclical.

The demand side is not relenting. Data-center electricity consumption surged 17% in 2025, driven by artificial-intelligence workloads, and the IEA projects that figure to double by 2030. Demand for generator step-up transformers — units that connect power plants and data-center campuses to the high-voltage transmission grid — has risen 274% since 2019. In April 2026, President Trump invoked five presidential determinations under the **Defense Production Act** to prioritize transformer manufacturing, framing the grid's fragility as a national security vulnerability. The roughly $323 million in available DPA funding is modest measured against a deficit of that scale.

The crisis looks purpose-built for Cleveland-Cliffs, but the company's response has been complicated by its own balance sheet. A $150 million transformer assembly plant announced in July 2024 for Weirton, West Virginia — which would have reactivated an idled tinplate facility and employed 600 steelworkers — was cancelled in May 2025 after a joint-venture partner withdrew and Cleveland-Cliffs reported a $483 million quarterly loss. Goncalves acknowledged the bind plainly: “I can't build the plant alone. I don't have the licensing and I don't have the IP.” The durable investment is happening upstream instead. In April 2026, Cleveland-Cliffs won final local approval for a **$195 million expansion at Butler Works** in Pennsylvania — adding roughly 25,000 net tons of annual GOES capacity, a roughly 10% increase — with production targeted for mid-2028 and partial backing from a $75 million Department of Energy grant.

For investors treating the GOES monopoly as a simple competitive moat, Cleveland-Cliffs' broader financials are a complicating layer. The company posted a full-year 2025 net loss of $1.48 billion, driven primarily by weak pricing in its much larger automotive flat-rolled segment; GOES results are not separately reported. First-quarter 2026 revenue came in at $4.9 billion against a net loss of $229 million. More structurally, the moat is policy-contingent: it rests on *Section 232* trade enforcement — tariffs on both raw electrical steel and downstream transformer laminations — in force since 2020 but carrying no permanent legislative guarantee. The thirty-year consolidation of U.S. electrical-steel capacity from dozens of mills to one plant complex is as much a story of trade vulnerability as of industrial staying power.

concepts.definition: A specialty silicon-iron alloy produced by rolling steel under carefully controlled conditions so that the metal's crystalline grains align in one direction. That alignment dramatically reduces the energy lost as heat when magnetic flux passes through a transformer core, making GOES the material of choice for high-efficiency power and distribution transformers. It is distinct from non-oriented electrical steel, which is used in electric motors and generators where flux direction changes constantly.

A large power transformer that raises the voltage produced by a generator — typically in the tens of kilovolts range — to the much higher voltages required for long-distance transmission on the high-voltage grid. Every power plant, large wind farm, utility-scale solar installation, and major data-center interconnect requires at least one GSU. They are among the most constrained items in the current supply shortage, with lead times now exceeding three years for many configurations.

A 1950 U.S. law that gives the president authority to direct industrial resources — factories, materials, supply chains — toward national defense priorities. Section 303 specifically allows the government to make loans, purchase commitments, and other investments to expand domestic production of critical goods. It has been invoked for COVID vaccines, semiconductor equipment, and, in April 2026, power transformer supply chains.

A provision of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 that allows the U.S. president to impose tariffs or quotas on imports determined to threaten national security. The Trump administration used it in 2018 to impose broad tariffs on imported steel and aluminum. A 2020 Section 232 action extended the regime to transformer laminations and cores made from electrical steel, closing a loophole that foreign producers had used to avoid the original steel tariffs.

The smaller class of transformer found on utility poles and in neighborhood substations, stepping medium-voltage power down to the 120–240 volt levels used in homes and businesses. Produced in far higher volumes than large power transformers, distribution units are also experiencing significant supply shortfalls — a 10% deficit in 2025 according to Wood Mackenzie — driven by aging installed infrastructure and rising electrification demand.

article.fact_check: The tweet's claim that Cleveland-Cliffs is building a transformer plant in West Virginia “coming online this year” is no longer accurate. The $150 million Weirton, West Virginia facility was announced in July 2024 with a 2025–2026 target, but Cleveland-Cliffs cancelled the project in May 2025 after a joint-venture partner withdrew and the company reported a $483 million quarterly net loss; no federal funding had been disbursed before the cancellation. The related claims — that Cleveland-Cliffs is the sole North American GOES producer and that U.S. transformer lead times are two to four years — are both accurate.

ticker_clf.name: Cleveland-Cliffs Inc.
ticker_clf.blurb: Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. is a major integrated steel producer operating in the United States and Canada, founded in 1847 and employing approximately 25,000 people. The company manufactures a broad range of flat-rolled steel products — including hot-rolled, cold-rolled, coated sheet, stainless, electrical, and plate products — serving primarily automotive and industrial customers. It also produces upstream raw materials such as iron ore, HBI, coal, and coke, and downstream non-steelmaking goods including stamped components, tubing, and tool-and-die products.
ticker_clf.recent: In October 2025, Cleveland-Cliffs executed what analysts described as a 'transformative deal' tied to Trump-era steel tariffs, triggering a sharp stock surge. As of mid-May 2026, shares trade near $10.99 — within a 52-week range of $5.63 to $16.70 — reflecting elevated volatility (beta 2.01) and a trailing net loss of approximately $1.22 billion on $18.9 billion in revenue. The company reported its most recent quarterly results on April 20, 2026; analyst consensus is Hold with a price target of $10.43.
